newsitem.title: USA: Hughes willing to spend big on aerospace.
newsitem.headline: Hughes willing to spend big on aerospace.

text.p: Hughes Electronics Corp. Chief Executive Mike Armstrong said Hughes is willing to make a multibillion-dollar acquisition to keep its place in the rapidly consolidating aerospace and defense industry.

"In a consolidating industry, unless you participate, you will not maintain your competitiveness," Armstrong said in an interview. "I don't think a week goes by that we don't have a meeting about buying something or selling something."
Asked whether he is weighing a large acquisition worth several billion dollars or smaller niche buys, he replied, "We consider all of the above."
Best known for satellites, Hughes makes everything from car stereos to missiles.

Armstrong said Hughes had looked at buying the aerospace and defense operations of Rockwell International Corp., which were sold to Boeing Co. for $3.2 billion, and at the military electronics business of Westinghouse Electric Corp., which sold for $3.5 billion to Northrop Grumman Corp.

"(We) made an assessment as to whether Rockwell was a good fit and we concluded that Rockwell ... was not a particularly good fit. It was a synergy issue. We looked at Westinghouse and in that case it was a price issue," he said.
Noting that Hughes is cash-rich and low on debt, analysts view the defense business of Raytheon Co. as a viable acquisition for the Los Angeles-based conglomerate.
"I think Hughes has great technology, so does Raytheon. It would be a great fit," said John Modzelewski of PaineWebber. "It would be a match made in heaven."
Modzelewski estimates Raytheon's defense unit could fetch some $7.0 billion, making it a difficult deal to pull off but a possiblility if done as a cash, stock and debt transaction.

Hughes is beginning to reap dividends from a restructuring plan put in place in 1992 which saw the company cut thousands of jobs, abandon 6.7 million square feet of property, cut two management levels and reduce costs by 40 percent in two years.

With a record satellite backlog of 40 orders, Hughes is seeking "several thousand" new employees, including 1,200 in its space division. Armstrong says he needs those people "just as fast as we can hire and train them."

With the satellite industry growing at some 10 percent annually, Hughes has no intention of relinquishing the No. 1 position it has held in that market since launching the first synchronous satellite in 1963.
That position is being pressured by archrival Lockheed-Martin Corp., which is constructing a $1.0 billion state-of-the-art satellite factory in California that will incorporate assembly line methods.
"I still look at what Lockheed Martin is doing in building a new factory and I worry that we've got to keep moving and never stand still because they're going to show up and be competitive," he said.
"You either invest or divest," Armstrong said. "One thing we don't do is stand still."
